children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK
The U.S. economy keeps powering through inflation and higher borrowing costs, defying a run up in Treasury yields and a Fed rate hike. That's what has the bond market spooked.

The usual economic brakes aren't slowing growth, hiring or an AI investment boom that looks unstoppable. That momentum helps explain investors' current predicament: The yield on the 10-year Treasury note this week hit highs not seen in nearly 20 years.

Meanwhile, in Washington, President Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a landmark summit-Xi's first visit to the capital in over a decade. Though Trump called it a "great meeting," our chief China correspondent Lingling Wei notes the summit papered over substantive differences between the two great powers-and left the competitive U.S.-China dynamic intact.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES
Tech titans including Jeff Bezos, Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg joined top U.S. officials at the White House for an elaborate state dinner capping Trump's summit with Xi.
Jeff Bezos has invested $30 billion in Blue Origin since its founding in 2000, an extraordinary commitment from the Amazon.com founder.
Efforts to rekindle talks to end the war between the U.S. and Iran are running into resistance from major Persian Gulf oil producers.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill has called for the resignation of Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell after an independent investigation found that he made a sexual comment to a staffer and tried to get a promotion for a romantic partner.
Thélyson Orélien's debut novel, "C'était ça ou Mourir" ("It Was Either That or Die"), was a literary triumph. Now, Orélien stands accused of using artificial intelligence to write the book.
3. LIVE FROM THE MARKETS
Follow our live financial coverage all day.

Stocks Spencer Jakab is watching: How rough has it been for owners of long-term Treasury debt? The most popular way for retail investors to gain exposure to them has been TLT, the iShares 20 Year+ Treasury Bond exchange-traded fund, which has attracted tens of billions of dollars in inflows. It hit a fresh all-time low Thursday, closing below $80 for the first time. Its price is down 46% in the past five years. So much for super safe bonds. (Get Spencer's Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox.)
Bond traders are paying too much attention to the oil price, writes James Mackintosh.

While wellness influencers tout peptides for muscle recovery, for investors, the real opportunity lies in pill-form treatments that could hit big pharma's most profitable franchises, writes David Wainer.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Did Putin really think our foreign correspondent was a spy?

In March 2023, while interviewing a source in the Russian city Yekaterinburg, WSJ reporter Evan Gershkovich was seized by Russian security services, falsely accused of being a U.S. spy, and thrown into Moscow's infamous Lefortovo prison. After 16 months in prison-and a global campaign for his release-Evan was finally freed in August 2024, in the largest East-West prisoner swap since the Cold War. Now, in an exclusive excerpt from his new book, "This Cursed Beautiful Land," Evan recounts the moment of his arrest, and the question that has stayed with him ever since.
A new tier of almost-premium credit cards is courting the not-quite-rich.

It used to be that $500 would get you a premium credit card. Now it gets you something just below that. The popularity of ultra-luxe cards with ever-higher annual fees has led to a reshuffling of the market, with cards just below that tier now making up a new category for the not-quite-rich enough. These near-premium cards are increasingly aimed at younger Americans eager for travel, dining out and the merry-go-round of other life experiences constantly on display on social media and in pop culture, report Ben Glickman and Jasmine Li.

6. SEE THE STORY
America's newest trophy asset is a country home in the Cotswolds.

The Cotswolds, a famed stretch of English countryside known for its rolling hills, picturesque villages and posh private schools, is drawing more American buyers. Prince Harry and his wife Meghan Markle, Duchess of Sussex, have recently put the region in the spotlight with their return to the U.K. The Cotswolds-and the up-and-coming "Notswolds"-are attractive to buyers for their scenery and proximity to London. And with thousands of square miles, it contains a variety of different villages, price points and housing types, from palaces to modern, boxy flats.
7. HAPPENING TODAY
Trump and first lady Melania Trump host Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for tea at the White House before visiting the National Archives, concluding Xi's state visit.
The U.N. holds a high-level meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response as the General Assembly's general debate continues in New York.
Today's paper
8. THE NUMBER

The estimated tuition reduction announced by Iowa's Coe College, bringing its price down to $31,850 starting next fall. More private colleges are reassessing their high sticker prices as more families balk at costs. While families have long associated price with quality, higher-ed analysts say that posture might be shifting.
9. AND FINALLY...
An iced coffee in a job interview sparked a raging etiquette debate.

What would you think if a candidate walked into a job interview with an iced coffee? That simple question has sparked debate about workplace decorum, highlighting changing expectations of professionalism. Proponents say it's a way to show their personality-and after all, it's just a drink. For iced-coffee critics, the problem is what the beverage signals: casualness, poor preparation and bad time management. Recruiters, job seekers and career coaches all have weighed in on the potential indignities of an iced beverage.
